title: Roy Benavidez — Six Hours in Hell
sources: Wikipedia: Roy Benavidez (5 August 1935 – 29 November 1998) — Texas-born son of a Mexican farmer and a Yaqui mother, orphaned young; Army Special Forces (5th Special Forces Group); in Vietnam in 1965 he stepped on a land mine and doctors said he would never walk again; at night, against doctors' orders, he crawled to the wall and taught himself to stand; walked out of hospital in July 1966 and returned to Vietnam in January 1968; on 2 May 1968 a 12-man Special Forces patrol west of Loc Ninh was surrounded by an NVA battalion; helicopters could not land; Benavidez voluntarily boarded one, jumped out armed only with a knife and carrying his medical bag, and ran about 75 m under fire; wounded in the leg, face and head; carried and dragged wounded men to the helicopter; the pilot was mortally wounded and the helicopter crashed; he pulled survivors from the wreck, handed out water and ammunition and called in air strikes; clubbed from behind, he killed his attacker in hand-to-hand combat; saved at least eight men; 37 bullet, bayonet and shrapnel wounds in a six-hour fight; thought dead and placed in a body bag, he spat in the doctor's face as it was being zipped up; the Medal of Honor was refused for lack of a living eyewitness; his radioman Brian O'Connor, whom he believed dead, read about him in a newspaper in Australia in 1980 and supplied the account; President Reagan presented the Medal of Honor on 24 February 1981, saying 'If the story of his heroism were a movie script, you would not believe it'

Photos (public domain, Wikimedia Commons / US Army / White House Photographic Office / US National Archives): Master Sergeant Roy Benavidez; the Medal of Honor ceremony at the Pentagon, 24 February 1981; 5th Special Forces Group in Vietnam; UH-1 Huey helicopters; US soldiers in Vietnam
Archive film (public domain): 'Operation San Angelo, 1st Brigade, 101st Airborne Division 1968' (US Army) — helicopters and jungle patrols in Vietnam, 1968 — illustrative, not Benavidez's mission
Music: Battle Hymn of the Republic — United States Air Forces in Europe Band, public domain

post.facebook:
He had 37 wounds, and they zipped him into a body bag. He was still alive.

Roy Benavidez, a Green Beret from Texas, stepped on a land mine in Vietnam in 1965. Doctors said he'd never walk again — so at night, against orders, he crawled out of bed and taught himself to stand. He walked out of the hospital and went straight back to Vietnam.

On 2 May 1968 a 12-man team was trapped in the jungle by an enemy battalion. Helicopters couldn't land. Benavidez jumped aboard one anyway, leapt out with a knife and a medical bag, and ran into the gunfire. Shot in the leg, the face and the head, he kept dragging the wounded to the helicopter. Then the pilot was killed and it crashed. He pulled the survivors out, called in air strikes, handed out water and ammunition, and won a hand-to-hand fight. Six hours later, at least eight men were alive because of him.

Back at base they thought he was dead. As the doctor zipped up the body bag, Benavidez spat in his face.

The Army refused him the Medal of Honor for years — there was no living witness. Then his radioman, whom he believed dead, read about him in a newspaper in Australia. In 1981 President Reagan gave him the medal: "If the story of his heroism were a movie script, you would not believe it."

youtube.description:
He had 37 wounds, and they zipped him into a body bag. He was still alive.

Green Beret Roy Benavidez was told he would never walk again after a land mine in 1965. On 2 May 1968 he jumped from a helicopter west of Loc Ninh, Vietnam, armed with a knife and a medical bag, and in six hours of fighting saved at least eight men. Thought dead, he spat in the doctor's face as the body bag was zipped. A radioman he believed dead later read about him in Australia and became the witness that won him the Medal of Honor, presented by President Reagan in 1981.
